Can Professional Air Polishing Be Used Around Dental Implants?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you have dental implants, you may have wondered what happens during your routine hygiene appointments. Perhaps your dental hygienist has mentioned air polishing, or you've noticed that your care feels slightly different now that you have an implant. Many patients search online for reassurance about whether air polishing around dental implants is safe, effective, and appropriate as part of their ongoing maintenance.

This is an entirely reasonable question. Dental implants are a significant investment in your oral health, and understanding how to care for them — including what professional treatments are suitable — is an important part of long-term success.

This article explains what air polishing involves, how it differs from traditional cleaning methods, what the current evidence suggests about its use around implants, and when speaking with a qualified dental professional may be beneficial. If you have specific concerns about your own implants, a clinical assessment is always the most reliable way to receive guidance tailored to your situation.

Can Air Polishing Be Safely Used Around Dental Implants?

Air polishing can be used around dental implants, but the type of powder and technique matter significantly. Conventional sodium bicarbonate powders are generally considered unsuitable near implant surfaces. Glycine-based or erythritol powders are widely used in clinical practice as gentler alternatives. Suitability always depends on individual clinical assessment by a qualified dental professional.

What Is Air Polishing and How Does It Work?

Air polishing is a professional dental cleaning technique that uses a pressurised stream of air, water, and a fine powder to remove staining, soft deposits, and biofilm from tooth surfaces. It has been used in general dental practice for several decades and is particularly popular for removing superficial stains caused by coffee, tea, red wine, or tobacco.

During an air polishing procedure, a handheld device directs a controlled jet of powder particles onto the tooth surface. The abrasive action of the powder, combined with the force of air and water, dislodges plaque and staining without the physical scraping associated with traditional scaling instruments.

Traditional air polishing powders — most commonly sodium bicarbonate — are relatively coarse and can be highly effective on natural tooth enamel. However, because implant surfaces, the surrounding soft tissues, and supporting bone structures have different characteristics compared to natural teeth, the conventional approach requires modification when implants are present.

In recent years, newer, finer powders — including glycine and erythritol — have been developed specifically to address delicate areas of the mouth, including peri-implant sites. These powders are gentler, less abrasive, and considered more appropriate for use around implant components and the surrounding gingival tissue.

How Dental Implants Differ From Natural Teeth

Understanding why implant maintenance requires careful consideration begins with an appreciation of how implants differ from natural teeth.

A natural tooth is anchored in the jawbone by the periodontal ligament — a network of fibrous tissue that acts as a shock absorber and plays a role in sensory feedback. Dental implants, by contrast, are titanium posts that osseointegrate directly into the jawbone. This means there is no periodontal ligament present. The implant is surrounded by what is known as the peri-implant tissue, which includes the mucosa (soft tissue) and the underlying bone.

The surface of a titanium implant is often intentionally textured at a microscopic level to encourage bone attachment during the healing phase. However, this texture also means that certain cleaning powders or instruments can potentially alter the implant surface in ways that might affect the long-term stability of the surrounding tissues.

Additionally, the junction between the implant crown and the implant body — or the abutment — can be a site where biofilm accumulates. Disrupting this biofilm effectively, without causing damage to the implant components or surrounding tissue, is one of the central challenges of implant maintenance.

For further detail on how single tooth implants are placed and maintained, understanding the structure of the implant system can help you ask informed questions at your next appointment.

The Role of Biofilm in Peri-Implant Health

One of the key reasons air polishing is discussed in the context of implant care is the management of biofilm — the structured community of bacteria that forms on all oral surfaces, including implant components.

Biofilm is not simply plaque in the traditional sense. It is a highly organised biological community that can be difficult to disrupt using standard brushing alone. When biofilm accumulates at the peri-implant sulcus — the crevice between the gum tissue and the implant — it can lead to inflammation of the surrounding tissue. This condition is known as peri-implant mucositis.

If left unaddressed, peri-implant mucositis can, in some cases, progress to peri-implantitis — a more serious condition involving inflammation and bone loss around the implant. This is clinically analogous to periodontitis around natural teeth, though the two conditions have distinct characteristics. Patients are often surprised that implant problems can progress without obvious pain.

Disrupting and removing biofilm at peri-implant sites during professional maintenance appointments is therefore an important part of protecting the long-term health of the implant. Air polishing using appropriate powders has been studied as a method of achieving thorough biofilm removal in these areas without the need for direct physical contact with the implant surface.

Which Air Polishing Powders Are Considered Appropriate Around Implants?

The choice of powder is central to the question of whether air polishing is appropriate near dental implants.

Sodium bicarbonate (traditional): This is a relatively coarse powder that works well on natural enamel. It is generally considered unsuitable for use directly around implant surfaces, restorations, or the peri-implant sulcus, due to its abrasive nature and potential to damage soft tissues at higher concentrations.

Glycine powder: Glycine is an amino acid-based powder that is significantly finer than sodium bicarbonate. Studies have explored its use in subgingival (below the gumline) applications, and it has been used specifically for peri-implant biofilm removal. Its gentler abrasive action is considered less likely to cause surface damage to implant components or trauma to the surrounding tissue.

Erythritol powder: An even finer option, erythritol-based powders have gained attention in recent years for use in both subgingival cleaning and implant maintenance. Some research has suggested that erythritol may have additional antimicrobial properties that support oral health.

The selection of the appropriate powder, combined with correct technique and equipment calibration, is a clinical decision made by the dental hygienist or clinician based on your individual oral health status.

What Does the Evidence Say About Air Polishing for Implant Maintenance?

The body of evidence examining air polishing for implant maintenance has grown considerably over the past decade. A number of clinical studies and systematic reviews have evaluated the effectiveness of glycine and erythritol powders for peri-implant biofilm management, with broadly positive findings in terms of biofilm disruption and patient comfort.

Several studies have found that subgingival air polishing using fine powders can be effective at reducing inflammation markers in peri-implant mucositis, particularly when used as part of a structured maintenance programme alongside other professional cleaning methods.

It is worth noting, however, that the evidence base — while encouraging — is still evolving. Study designs vary, follow-up periods differ, and the clinical outcomes observed may not translate uniformly to every patient or implant type. This underlines the importance of individualised clinical judgement rather than a single standardised approach applicable to all patients.

Current guidance from professional bodies and leading clinicians suggests that air polishing with appropriate powders can be a useful adjunct in implant maintenance, but it should be used in combination with other professional techniques and as part of a structured, personalised recall programme.

Clinical Explanation: Understanding the Peri-Implant Environment

To appreciate why implant maintenance differs from standard dental cleaning, it helps to understand a little about the biological environment that surrounds an implant.

Around a natural tooth, the gum tissue attaches to the tooth surface via a combination of epithelial attachment and connective tissue fibres. This biological seal provides a degree of natural defence against bacterial invasion.

Around a dental implant, the attachment mechanism is different. The peri-implant mucosa forms a biological seal, but the connective tissue fibres run parallel to the implant surface rather than attaching into it as they do around natural teeth. This structural difference means that the peri-implant seal may be less resilient to bacterial penetration, and disruption of the sulcular tissue during cleaning should be approached with care.

The titanium surface of the implant body is generally biocompatible, but if it becomes exposed due to bone loss, it can become colonised by bacteria in a manner that is particularly difficult to treat. Maintaining the health of the surrounding soft and hard tissues through regular, appropriate professional care is therefore an important preventative measure.

When Professional Assessment May Be Appropriate

If you have dental implants and are experiencing any of the following, it is advisable to seek a professional dental evaluation at an appropriate time:

  • Bleeding around the implant during brushing or at other times — this may indicate inflammation of the surrounding tissue
  • Swelling, redness, or tenderness in the gum tissue near the implant
  • A sensation that the implant feels different — loose, uncomfortable, or altered in any way
  • Difficulty cleaning around the implant despite regular home care
  • Uncertainty about your current maintenance regime and whether it is appropriate for your implant type

None of these situations should cause alarm, but they do suggest that a professional review would be beneficial. Early identification of any changes around an implant is associated with better outcomes compared to delayed assessment.

If you have questions about implant aftercare and long-term maintenance, a member of the clinical team will be able to advise you on what to expect during your hygiene appointments.

What to Expect During an Implant Hygiene Appointment

A professional maintenance appointment for dental implants may look somewhat different from a standard hygiene visit. Your clinician will typically begin with an assessment of the peri-implant tissue, checking for signs of inflammation, probing depths around the implant, and reviewing any radiographs if indicated.

Cleaning around implants is usually carried out using instruments that are designed to avoid scratching the titanium or ceramic surfaces of the implant components. These may include:

  • Plastic or carbon fibre-tipped scalers — designed to remove deposits without scratching metal surfaces
  • Ultrasonic devices with specialised implant tips — using vibration and water to dislodge biofilm
  • Air polishing with glycine or erythritol powder — for thorough biofilm removal in the peri-implant sulcus
  • Polishing with non-abrasive paste — to finish and smooth crown surfaces where appropriate

The frequency of your maintenance appointments will depend on your individual risk profile, the health of your peri-implant tissues, and your clinician's recommendations. Many patients with implants attend for professional cleaning every three to four months rather than the standard six-month interval, particularly in the first years after implant placement.

Prevention and Ongoing Oral Health Advice for Implant Patients

Maintaining the health of your dental implants between professional appointments is equally important. Here are some evidence-informed suggestions that may support peri-implant health:

  • Brush twice daily using a soft-bristled or electric toothbrush. Pay attention to the gum margin around the implant crown.
  • Use interdental brushes sized appropriately for the spaces around your implant. Your hygienist can advise on the correct size.
  • Consider a water flosser (oral irrigator) as an adjunct to your cleaning routine. These devices can be particularly helpful for cleaning around implant crowns and bridge frameworks.
  • Avoid abrasive toothpastes — heavily abrasive formulas are generally unnecessary for implant crowns and may, over time, dull their surface.
  • Attend your recall appointments as recommended, even when your implant feels comfortable and problem-free.
  • Avoid smoking — tobacco use is one of the most consistently identified risk factors for peri-implant disease and implant failure.
  • Communicate openly with your dental team about any changes you notice, however minor they may seem.

For patients with dental bridges or implant-supported restorations, specific cleaning techniques may be required and can be discussed during your appointment.

Key Points to Remember

  • Air polishing can be used around dental implants, but the choice of powder matters significantly. Fine powders such as glycine and erythritol are generally preferred over traditional sodium bicarbonate near implant components.
  • The peri-implant environment is biologically different from that surrounding natural teeth, which is why implant-specific maintenance approaches are necessary.
  • Biofilm management is central to long-term implant health. Disrupting biofilm at peri-implant sites helps reduce the risk of peri-implant mucositis and peri-implantitis.
  • Clinical evidence supports the use of modern air polishing powders as part of implant maintenance, though individual suitability depends on clinical assessment.
  • Regular professional maintenance appointments — often more frequent than for natural teeth — are an important part of protecting your implant long term.
  • Home care habits including careful brushing, interdental cleaning, and avoiding tobacco contribute significantly to peri-implant health between appointments.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is air polishing safe for dental implants?

Air polishing can be appropriate for use around dental implants when the correct powder and technique are used. Traditional sodium bicarbonate powders are generally considered unsuitable near implant surfaces due to their coarser, more abrasive nature. Finer powders such as glycine or erythritol have been more widely adopted for peri-implant maintenance. The suitability of any cleaning method for your specific implant should be discussed with and determined by your dental hygienist or dentist during a clinical assessment.

How often should dental implants be professionally cleaned?

The recommended frequency of professional cleaning for dental implants varies depending on individual circumstances, including the health of the surrounding tissue, your home care routine, and any other risk factors. Many clinicians recommend three to four monthly appointments for implant patients, particularly in the early years after placement. Your dental team will advise you on the most appropriate recall interval based on your clinical needs. It is important to attend these appointments even when the implant feels comfortable and causes no problems.

Can I have a standard hygiene appointment if I have implants?

You can attend a hygiene appointment, but it is important to inform your hygienist that you have dental implants so that appropriate instruments and techniques can be used. Standard metal scalers and certain pastes are not recommended for use directly on implant components, as they can scratch titanium or ceramic surfaces. A hygienist experienced in implant maintenance will adapt their approach accordingly, using implant-safe instruments and, where suitable, appropriate air polishing powders.

What are the early signs that something may be wrong around a dental implant?

Some signs that warrant professional attention include bleeding around the implant during brushing, swelling or redness of the surrounding gum tissue, tenderness or discomfort in the area, or any sensation that the implant feels different from usual. These signs do not necessarily indicate a serious problem, but they suggest that a clinical review would be beneficial. Early assessment generally leads to better outcomes, so it is advisable not to delay seeking advice if you notice changes around your implant.

Will air polishing damage the surface of my implant crown?

When the correct powder, technique, and equipment are used, air polishing should not damage implant crowns made from ceramic or zirconia materials. However, technique matters significantly, and it is important that the procedure is carried out by a trained clinician familiar with implant maintenance. The level of abrasiveness of the powder used, the distance and angle of the device, and the duration of application are all factors that a skilled clinician will consider carefully during your appointment.

What is peri-implant mucositis and how is it related to cleaning?

Peri-implant mucositis is inflammation of the soft tissue (mucosa) surrounding a dental implant, caused by the accumulation of bacterial biofilm. It is considered a reversible condition if identified and treated promptly, typically through professional cleaning and improved home care. If left unaddressed, peri-implant mucositis can, in some cases, progress to peri-implantitis, which involves bone loss around the implant. Regular professional maintenance, including effective biofilm removal at peri-implant sites, plays an important role in preventing and managing this condition.

Conclusion

Air polishing around dental implants is a clinically relevant topic for anyone who has undergone implant treatment or is considering it. The short answer is that air polishing can be used appropriately near implants — provided the right powder is selected, the technique is properly applied, and the decision is made by a qualified clinician based on individual clinical circumstances.

Modern fine powders such as glycine and erythritol have expanded the possibilities for professional peri-implant maintenance, offering gentler biofilm removal that supports the long-term health of the surrounding tissue. Understanding the biological differences between natural teeth and implants helps explain why implant-specific care approaches are necessary, and why attending regular maintenance appointments with a clinician experienced in implant aftercare is so important — even when symptoms seem absent, as discussed in why maintenance appointments matter even when an implant feels fine.

If you have questions about your implant maintenance routine, or if you have noticed any changes around your implant, speaking with a dental professional is always the most appropriate next step. Air polishing around dental implants is just one component of a broader maintenance strategy — one that works best when combined with thorough home care and regular professional assessment.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

In the UK, you can check whether your treating clinician is registered with the General Dental Council (GDC), and whether the provider is regulated by the Care Quality Commission (CQC), where applicable. Treatment suitability and outcomes vary by individual, and no result can be guaranteed.
